abstract: Autor and Thompson introduce a formal model of expertise — the costly-to-acquire, imperfectly transferable judgment, creativity, and tacit knowledge that certain tasks demand — and analyze how AI interacts with it. The model posits that while AI can readily automate routine and codifiable tasks, expertise-intensive tasks create a natural floor on human labor demand because the underlying knowledge is inherently difficult to replicate or transfer to machines. The key tension: occupations requiring substantial expertise are more resilient to AI displacement, but AI tools simultaneously erode the premium on expertise by making novices substantially more productive. Calibrated to US occupational data, the paper finds that approximately 30% of employment involves high-expertise tasks with strong human complementarity. Empirical evidence suggests AI-assisted novices can achieve 60-80% of expert performance on structured tasks, raising fundamental questions about the long-run value of deep expertise in an AI-augmented economy. The framework helps explain why AI's labor market effects are highly heterogeneous across occupations and why predictions of mass unemployment may be overstated for expertise-heavy roles, while also highlighting that expertise premiums may narrow considerably as AI democratizes access to previously scarce capabilities.
keyFindings: Approximately 30% of US employment involves high-expertise tasks with strong human complementarity, creating resilience to AI displacement
AI-assisted novices can achieve 60-80% of expert performance on structured tasks, potentially eroding expertise premiums
Expertise-intensive occupations are more resilient to AI displacement but face premium compression rather than job elimination
The model predicts highly heterogeneous AI effects across occupations, depending on expertise requirements
Mass unemployment predictions may be overstated for expertise-heavy roles, but expertise premiums are likely to narrow
methodology: Formal economic model of expertise acquisition and AI substitution, calibrated to US occupational data from O*NET and BLS. Empirical calibration uses task-level expertise classifications and observed AI-assisted performance data from experimental studies. Theoretical framework distinguishes routine tasks (AI-substitutable) from expertise-intensive tasks (human-complementary).
qualifiers: Model is theoretical with empirical calibration rather than direct causal estimation. The 60-80% novice performance finding is drawn from structured tasks and may not generalize to unstructured or creative domains. Does not account for potential AI improvements that could eventually replicate tacit knowledge. US occupational structure may differ from other economies. Long-run dynamics of expertise premium erosion are projected, not observed.
